title: Design a data structure that accepts a continuous stream of numbers and can return the median of all numbers seen so far at any time. Insertion and median-query should both be efficient. Explain the two-heap technique.
shortTitle: Find the Median of a Number Stream (Two Heaps)
keyPoints: Use a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, keeping their sizes within one of each other.
The median is the top of the larger heap when sizes differ, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal.
Each insertion costs O(log n) for heap operations, and each median query costs O(1) by peeking at the tops.
Rebalancing after each insertion ensures the size invariant is always maintained.
For banking amounts, use BigDecimal with a reverse-order comparator on the max-heap and controlled rounding for the average.
This is far superior to re-sorting the stream on every query, which would cost O(n log n) per query.

s1_definition.oneliner: Split the stream into a smaller half in a max-heap and a larger half in a min-heap, keep them balanced, and the median lives at the boundary between the two tops.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Max-heap (smaller half)** – holds the lower half of all numbers, with the largest of them at the root for quick access.
- **Min-heap (larger half)** – holds the upper half of all numbers, with the smallest of them at the root.
- **Balance invariant** – the two heaps differ in size by at most one, so the boundary between them is always the median.
- **Median query** – when sizes are equal, the median is the average of the two roots; when one heap is larger, its root is the median.
- **Insertion** – each new number is placed in the correct heap based on the current max-heap root, then rebalanced if needed.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day and the risk team wants the running median at any moment to spot drift. They split all amounts into two buckets: a low bucket (max-heap) holding the smaller half with its largest value on top, and a high bucket (min-heap) holding the larger half with its smallest value on top. The median sits right at the boundary between the two buckets.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the median of a number stream is the textbook two-heap problem. You keep a max-heap that holds the smaller half of all numbers and a min-heap that holds the larger half, and you keep their sizes within one of each other. The median then lives at the boundary: when the counts are equal it is the average of the two heap tops, and when they differ it is the top of the larger heap. Each insertion is a logarithmic heap operation and each median query is a constant-time peek.

The insertion rule is straightforward: if the new number is at most the max-heap root, it belongs in the smaller half; otherwise it belongs in the larger half. After each insertion you rebalance by moving a root across if one heap grew two larger than the other. This ensures the boundary always sits at the true median position.

At the National Bank of India, the risk team used this to maintain the running median transaction amount over a live stream, watching for drift in typical transaction sizes in real time. They stressed that amounts must be BigDecimal, so the max-heap used a reverse-order comparator and the even-count median was computed with BigDecimal division at a fixed scale and rounding mode, never floating-point, because money must stay exact.

The key advantage over re-sorting is performance: two heaps give O(n log n) total for n insertions with O(1) per query, while re-sorting gives O(n^2 log n) total. For a live stream of millions of transactions, that difference is the line between real-time and unusable.

Remember one sentence: smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap, balanced within one, and the median lives at the boundary between the two roots.
